key_claims: Bin Ladin and Zawahiri issued the February 1998 World Islamic Front fatwa from Afghanistan, though neither was an Islamic legal scholar.
Bin Ladin's calls to attack the United States date from 1992 and escalated through the 1996 and 1998 declarations.
Bin Ladin draws ideologically on Sayyid Qutb and selectively on Ibn Taimiyyah.
Bin Ladin framed the Afghan jihad against the Soviets as proof that Muslims could defeat a superpower.
Saudi-Iran competition and Pakistan's Islamist military regime fostered religious schools and fundamentalist influence.
Bin Ladin and Azzam founded al Qaeda in 1988 as a general headquarters for future jihad, and Bin Ladin became its undisputed emir after Azzam's assassination in November 1989.
Saudi and US aid to the Afghan rebels was funneled through Pakistan's ISID, while Bin Ladin relied on his own Golden Chain funding and received little or no US assistance.
Turabi's National Islamic Front hosted Bin Ladin in Sudan from 1991, where he built business fronts, procurement networks and an Islamic Army Shura to coordinate allied terrorist groups.
Al Qaeda built an international web of NGOs and offices (Zagreb, Sarajevo, Baku, Nairobi, Brooklyn al Khifa) that supported jihadist activity.

Bin Ladin supported or trained groups such as MILF, the Abu Sayyaf Brigade, JI, a Pakistani Kashmir group and Tajik Islamists, and al Qaeda reached a cooperative understanding with Iran and Hezbollah despite Sunni-Shia divisions.
Bin Ladin was one of many 'terrorist barons' in the early 1990s but stood out by targeting the 'far enemy', the United States.
Contacts between Bin Ladin and Iraq in Sudan produced no evidence of an Iraqi response, though Bin Ladin aided anti-Saddam Islamists in Kurdistan who later became Ansar al Islam.
Pakistan held the key to Bin Ladin's ability to use Afghanistan as a base; its military intelligence likely knew of and facilitated his 1996 return.
Pakistani intelligence reportedly introduced Bin Ladin to Taliban leaders in Kandahar, hoping to use Khowst camps for Kashmiri militants.
Mullah Omar's personal relationship with Bin Ladin shielded him from objections by other Taliban leaders.
Under Taliban protection al Qaeda gained sanctuary, free movement and state-linked logistics such as Ariana Airlines and Ministry of Defense plates.
An estimated 10,000-20,000 fighters trained in Bin Ladin-supported camps 1996-2001, but only a few hundred became al Qaeda members.
Al Qaeda merged effectively with Zawahiri's Egyptian Islamic Jihad and shifted to planning and executing its own operations.
Contacts between Bin Ladin and Iraq are reported, but the Commission found no evidence of a collaborative operational relationship.
Al-Qaeda began casing Nairobi embassy targets in December 1993 under Ali Mohamed, and Bin Ladin reviewed the reports by January 1994.
Kenya cell management passed from Banshiri (operational commander) through Fawwaz and Wadi al Hage to Harun Fazul.
Delay before the attack was due to disruptions including Bin Ladin's Sudan difficulties, move to Afghanistan, Taliban ties, and Banshiri's drowning.
The decision to launch the embassy attacks was apparently made by the time of the February 1998 fatwa, linked to the al-Qaeda–EIJ merger.

A joint al-Qaeda–EIJ office in Baku and Bin Ladin's London office handled claims of responsibility for the 7 August 1998 bombings, which killed 12 Americans and over 200 others in Nairobi and 11 in Dar es Salaam.
